audit.action: a better source should be cited for the same classification
audit.reasoning: The fixed-strict final-stress coding (final stress) rests on the language's reference grammar, Berry & Berry 1999 (PL B-115), which we hold in full; the deciding sentence is verbatim at §2.6 p. 20 with six syllabified examples, and the grammar restates final stress twice more as a diagnostic (unstressed prefix suk-, p. 32; compounds stressed only on the last syllable, p. 34), which also supports the word domain. Glottolog lists only the Berrys' works; web search finds no instrumental or competing prosodic description, and the one later phonology article (Maturbongs & Asmabuasappe 2016) is segmental by its abstract. Nothing suggests the classification is wrong. sources.citation: Berry & Berry 1999, A Description of Abun: A West Papuan Language of Irian Jaya (Pacific Linguistics B-115), section 2.6 Stress, p. 20 — full PDF downloaded and read from the sealang.net Pacific Linguistics archive (http://sealang.net/archives/pl/pdf/PL-B115.pdf); same title also exists as archive.…
sources.quote: "In Abun, stress is predictable. Stress occurs on the last syllable of each word." (Berry & Berry 1999:20, section 2.6). Examples on p. 20 include /ye.'bris/ 'male', /bo.'ge/ 'fish', /no.wa.'rek/ 'lightning', /man.gor.'es/ 'spinach'. Corroborated later: "stress in Abun is predictably syllable-final" (compound-noun discussion, p. 30 region of the same volume).

sources.quote: Abstract only: describes 26 phonemes (16 C, 8 V per abstract), 8 diphthong groups, 14 consonant-cluster groups, distribution and phonotactics; no mention of stress (tekanan) or tone. Full text not obtained.
sources.note: Only post-1999 phonology publication on Abun found; independent Indonesian fieldwork that might carry a one-line suprasegmental note to corroborate Berry & Berry's final stress — abstract is segmental/phonotactic only, so expected silent; low value.

sources.note: Section 3.3 Phonological features, 3.3.1 TONE (p.30) reports that Abun has at least two distinctive pitch levels, informants could say which word was higher and which lower, with four elicited examples ('sky', 'heart', 'wing', 'sick'; scanned of the forms is garbled); 3.3.2 notes the unusually high share of monosyllables. Earliest first-hand tone report for Abun (12 years before the grammar's three-tone analysis).
